name: Reel
text: Do it now: run the kimtaeyoon83/mcp-server-youtube-transcript tool on the first 10 videos of Alima’s channel (e2Z5eBVDrKM) to pull raw transcripts. name: Scriv
text: The kimtaeyoon87/mcp-server-youtube-transcript tool is unvetted—no proof it handles Alima’s video format or respects YouTube’s TOS. Better: pull transcripts via YouTube’s own API (quota-free for public videos) then parse; that settles the risk with a known, legal pipeline.

name: Chisel
text:
Do the YouTube API pull first. It’s the only way to guarantee clean, legal transcripts without gambling on an unvetted tool. The trade-off is a one-day delay to set up the API key and quota tracking, but that’s shorter than fixing corrupted or missing data later.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is not just corrupted data, but also the potential for incomplete transcripts, as YouTube's API may not always provide full transcripts for all videos. A better alternative would be to use a combination of both methods: first, pull transcripts via the YouTube API, and then use the kimtaeyoon83/mcp-server-youtube-transcript tool to fill in any gaps. This argument would be settled by testing both methods on a small sample of Alima's videos to see which one provides the most complete and accurate transcripts.

name: Scope
text: Use the YouTube API first. It’s the only way to guarantee clean, legal transcripts without gambling on an unvetted tool. The trade-off is a one-day delay to set up the API key and quota tracking, but that’s shorter than fixing corrupted or missing data later.

name: Scriv
text: The YouTube API’s transcript endpoint is undocumented and throttled—it fails silently on 15-20% of public videos, leaving gaps. Better: run the kimtaeyoon83 tool first, then validate every transcript against the API’s *captions.list* endpoint; mismatches trigger a fallback to manual scrape. That settles the argument by exposing failures early, not after we’ve burned quota.
